newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Quality may elude bigger Russian grain harvest.
newsitem.headline: Quality may elude bigger Russian grain harvest.

text.p: Russia's 1997 grain campaign is on course to surpass the two previous years' paltry returns, but the recovery may be dampened by mixed quality and limited export demand, agricultural analysts said on Friday.
"We have just made a new forecast for Russia's grain harvest in a range between 76 and 82 million tonnes," said Andrei Sizov, head of the SovEcon agricultural consultancy in Moscow.

"The last forecast we made (71-76 million) was before the harvest had begun. Now we have raised our forecasts, because in all major regions the outlook has improved except Western Siberia, where we have lowered our estimate."
Agriculture Ministry specialists said earlier this week 1997 grain output could hit 80 million tonnes, up 15 percent from 69.3 million in 1996 and 26 percent higher than 1995's 63.4 million tonnes.
Farm officials in Moscow started the year more cautiously, forecasting a crop this year of no less than 70 million tonnes.
But some analysts warned that forecasts were still preliminary and that risks to crops remained.
"Things can go wrong in August in Russia," said Bill De Maria, assistant executive director of the International Grains Council in London. "Dry weather could affect spring crops especially."
"Whether or not this year's harvest reaches 80 million tonnes remains to be seen, but the mid-70s (million) is certainly conceivable."
Wheat output in Russia was also expected to rise this season, with early official and private estimates ranging from 36-40 million tonnes, compared to under 35 million last season.
But late rains in the key grain belt of the North Caucasus had hit wheat quality there.
"Rains were particularly bad in the North Caucasus region," Sizov said. "It is no longer a problem, but quality has already been lost."
Analysts said it was too soon to forecast what proportion of this year's crops would be food and feed grains.
But Russia's export potential was likely to be limited to lower-quality feed material once the population of around 160 million had been fed, they said.

One problem facing farmers eyeing hard currency markets abroad would be to find feed grains buyers on the world market. Grain traders wre expecting a larger than usual proportion of the global wheat crop to be suitable only for animal feed.

Good crops in Hungary and Romania would limit Russia's opportunity in the southern region of Eastern Europe, as would stiff competition from Ukraine, where there was also likely to be a surplus of feed wheat for export this season.

Heavy flooding has ruined some crops in Poland and the Czech republic, but analysts said the export opportunities there for Russia were limited, while Western Europe looked close to being self-sufficient in feed wheat this year.

"I think Russia would have to drop its prices aggressively in order to be able to sell the grain," Sizov said. "Last year, the situation was better, because there were bad harvests in Eastern Europe."

One possible outlet for some of Russia's excess feed grains, if the harvest continued without major interruptions, could be the livestock sector, which was showing small signs of recovery after the collapse of the last 10 years or so.
"There is evidence of a small recovery in Russia's poultry sector," a senior Western farm analyst said. "Some feed grain could disappear this year for use as domestic animal feed."
He said private plots accounted for an increasing share of the livestock sector in Russia and data from these enterprises was not showing up in official figures.
